record.original_question: For a preemptive multiprocessor real-time system with implicit-deadline sporadic tasks and a specified total priority order on the tasks, determine whether global fixed-priority schedulability is decidable by an exact test and what its computational complexity is. The input is tau, m > 1 preemptive processors, and the priority assignment; the question is whether fixed-priority scheduling on m processors meets every deadline for every legal job-arrival sequence generated by tau.

evidence.quote: In fixed-priority (FP) scheduling, each task in τ is assigned a unique priority. All the task priorities are totally ordered
Problem 4 (Exact multiprocessor global EDF-schedulability — implicit-deadline tasks.) Input: Implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ . A positive integer m > 1.
The analog of Problem 4 with respect to FP scheduling — Given τ, m, and a priority assignment, is τ FP-schedulable on m processors under the given priority assignment? — is also open.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. An implicit-deadline sporadic task system is a finite set τ = {T_1, …, T_n} of tasks, where each task T_i = (C_i, P_i) consists of a worst-case execution time C_i > 0 and a period P_i ≥ C_i; its relative deadline equals P_i. A legal job-arrival sequence generated by τ produces, for each task T_i, an infinite stream of jobs such that consecutive jobs of T_i are released at least P_i time units apart; each released job requires up to C_i units of processor time and must complete by P_i time units after its release.

Global fixed-priority (FP) scheduling on m identical processors (m > 1, integer), under a given total priority order ≺ on the tasks, works as follows: at every instant the scheduler executes, on the m processors, the (up to) m active jobs whose tasks have highest priority under ≺; preemption and migration of jobs across processors are permitted at no cost. The system τ is said to be FP-schedulable on m processors under ≺ if, for every legal job-arrival sequence generated by τ, every job meets its deadline.

Problem. Given as input an implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ, an integer m > 1, and a total priority assignment on τ:

(a) Is the question "Is τ FP-schedulable on m processors under the given priority assignment?" decidable by an exact algorithm?

(b) If decidable, determine its computational complexity.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has established decidability of exact global fixed-priority schedulability for implicit-deadline sporadic tasks on identical multiprocessors by exhibiting a bounded "decidability interval" and a pre-order/simulation-based exact test, but the resulting algorithms are of very high complexity and only handle small systems (a handful of tasks/processors). The precise computational complexity (e.g., tight hardness classification) remains unresolved, so the problem is at best partially solved.

status_evidence.title: A pre-order relation for exact schedulability test of sporadic tasks on multiprocessor Global Fixed-Priority scheduling
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a pre-order relation enabling an exact schedulability test for sporadic tasks under global FP scheduling on multiprocessors.
status_evidence.claim: Decidability of the exact test has been established via simulation/pre-order techniques.

status_evidence.title: Towards a Tractable Exact Test for Global Multiprocessor Fixed Priority Scheduling
status_evidence.snippet: Even with improved approaches, complexity remains too high for task sets with more than about seven tasks and more than four processors.
status_evidence.claim: Exact complexity is not tightly settled and practical algorithms scale poorly.

status_evidence.title: Polynomial Exact Schedulability and Infeasibility Test for Fixed-Priority Scheduling on Multiprocessor Platforms
status_evidence.snippet: Polynomial-time exact tests are known only for restricted cases (e.g., n = m+1).
status_evidence.claim: General complexity classification is still open; only special cases are polynomial.
